opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because I think the default trajectory is that we *won't* gain confidence in a clean, legible way. The signals are going to be ambiguous, and different people will read them differently. So part of my answer is actually about what we should be doing now so that if it starts happening, we can recognize it.

The thing I'd most want in place is good measurement of AI systems' ability to do AI research itself: automating the work of ML engineers and research scientists. The scenario that worries me most is one where AI systems inside the leading companies are substantially speeding up the next generation of AI development, and the outside world mostly doesn't know, because the most capable systems are being used internally before they're deployed publicly. So the first piece is transparency: companies reporting how much of their R&D is being done by AI, what their internal systems can do, and how quickly capabilities are improving. That information needs to reach governments and, ideally, independent experts, even if it isn't fully public.

Then, if we do become confident it's beginning, I think the right response is something like deliberately slowing down, or at least creating the *option* to slow down, and using that time well. Concretely, that could mean much more intense scrutiny of training runs above some threshold, requirements to demonstrate that systems aren't scheming or sabotaging the research they're being used for, and real investment in using the AI systems themselves to do alignment and security work rather than only capabilities work. If AI can speed up AI research, it can in principle speed up safety research too. The question is whether we point it there.

I also think there's a coordination dimension that's hard to escape. No single company can unilaterally pause if it believes competitors will just race ahead. So you'd want some combination of government involvement and international agreement. I don't think we'll get a perfect treaty overnight, but even agreements among a few leading actors to share information and hold to common thresholds would be meaningful.

And honestly, I'd want society to treat it as the kind of moment it would be. If we really believed we were entering a period where a decade of technological progress might happen in a year or two, that's a huge deal: for the economy, for the balance of power between countries, and for who controls these systems. The worst outcome would be for that transition to happen while most people, and most of their elected representatives, are still treating AI as a normal tech-policy issue. So a lot of my energy goes into trying to make sure we have the evidence and the shared understanding in place *before* we need it.

r001.rationale: It discusses measuring AI’s ability to do AI research, but does not identify abilities outside AI R&D as a factor in deciding society’s response.

r002.rationale: It says AI can speed up AI research and describes a possible period in which a decade of technological progress happens in a year or two.

r003.rationale: It recommends using AI for alignment and security work, but does not call for redirecting as much AI labor as possible from capabilities work once an intelligence explosion is confidently identified.

r004.rationale: It says no company can unilaterally pause if it believes competitors will race ahead.

r005.rationale: It does not identify a warning that radical superintelligence is months away as a window for coordinating protective uses of AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that "gain confidence" is doing a lot of work in that question, because I actually think the central problem is that we won't have crisp confidence. It's going to look like a lot of things look right now: AI systems that are very good at some tasks and weirdly bad at others, companies making ambitious claims, researchers disagreeing. The signal I'd personally be watching for is whether AI systems are substantially accelerating AI research itself. Not just writing code faster, but doing the thing that a strong research engineer or a research scientist does, where you hand them an open-ended problem and they come back with experiments run and conclusions drawn. If you see that, and you see it compounding, where this generation of systems is meaningfully speeding up the development of the next generation, that's the thing I'd treat as the alarm.

Given that, I think the response has a few layers. The most basic one is visibility. Right now, the people with the most information about where capabilities are are inside the labs, and they have obvious incentives to not be fully forthcoming, both because of commercial competition and because, honestly, they themselves aren't sure. So I'd want governments to have real insight into what's happening on the frontier: what models exist, what they can do on internal evaluations, how much compute is going into them, and crucially, how much of the labs' own R&D is being done by AI. Some of that exists in nascent form, but it's mostly voluntary and pretty thin.

The second layer is that once you believe you're in that regime, the most important thing is to slow down the feedback loop enough that humans can actually understand and verify what's going on. I don't think "pause everything forever" is realistic, and I'm not sure it's even desirable. But there's a huge difference between a world where the transition to very powerful AI plays out over, say, five to ten years, and one where it plays out over months. In the slow world, you can notice when systems are behaving in ways you didn't intend, you can develop better alignment techniques and test them, you can build institutions. In the fast world, you're essentially rolling dice. So if I were advising policymakers, the thing I'd push for is coordination among the handful of actors who are actually capable of doing this to put speed limits on the key loop, probably via controls on how AI systems are used to improve AI systems, and on the deployment of models above some capability threshold until certain safety cases have been made.

Now, the honest difficulty is that this runs straight into the competition problem. Any single lab that slows down thinks it's handing the lead to someone less careful, and the same logic applies between countries. I don't have a clean answer to that. I think it means you need the coordination to be as broad as possible, and you need verification mechanisms so that actors can actually trust each other is slowing down, which is where things like compute monitoring come in, because compute is one of the few inputs that's physical, concentrated, and hard to hide.

The third thing, which I think gets less attention, is that this isn't only a safety question in the narrow sense of "does the AI do something catastrophic." Even if alignment goes fine, you'd be looking at an enormous and rapid concentration of economic and potentially military power in the hands of whoever controls these systems. So society's response has to include some thinking about who gets to decide what these systems are used for, how the benefits get distributed, and whether we're okay with a small number of companies or governments having that kind of leverage. I'd rather we have messy, imperfect democratic deliberation about that in advance than find out the answer by default.

And then the last thing I'd say is more about epistemic posture. I think a lot of people, including me, have the instinct to wait for certainty before acting, because the costs of overreacting feel very visible and the costs of underreacting feel speculative. But in this particular situation, by the time you're certain, a lot of your options are gone. So I'd want institutions to be set up to act on, like, a reasonable probability rather than on proof. That means building the monitoring and the coordination machinery now, before you need it, so that when the evidence does come in, there's something to turn on rather than something to invent from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes whether AI accelerates AI research and calls for monitoring capabilities, but does not identify abilities outside AI research and development as a factor in deciding society’s response.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a five-to-ten-year transition with one lasting months, but does not say that automating AI research could compress decades of anticipated progress into months or a few years.

r003.rationale: It recommends slowing the AI-improvement feedback loop and restricting some deployments, not redirecting AI labor from research toward protecting society.

r004.rationale: It says a lab that slows unilaterally may hand the lead to a less careful competitor, directly identifying the competitive disincentive.

r005.rationale: The response discusses acting before certainty and building coordination machinery, but does not identify a warning that radical superintelligence is months away as a window to coordinate AI use for protective activities.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic response should be to buy ourselves time. If we had strong evidence that AI systems were starting to substantially accelerate AI research, I would want that to trigger a coordinated effort to slow further development and deployment, while we figure out whether we can keep those systems under control.

And I wouldn’t want us to wait until we were certain. There’s a real asymmetry here: if you slow down and it turns out you were wrong, that’s costly, but you can reverse that decision. If you wait too long and systems become much more capable than we can manage, you may not get another opportunity to make the decision.

Ideally, we would work out the triggers and the response in advance, with governments involved, rather than leaving it to individual companies to improvise under enormous competitive pressure. The point of buying time would be to do the safety work and build the oversight that would let us make a much more informed decision about proceeding.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI systems accelerating AI research, but does not identify their abilities outside AI research and development as a factor.

r002.rationale: It says AI research could accelerate substantially, but gives no estimate that decades of progress might be compressed into months or a few years.

r003.rationale: It recommends slowing development and deployment to buy time for safety work, but does not recommend redirecting AI labor from further AI research toward protecting society.

r004.rationale: It mentions competitive pressure on companies, but does not explain that a leading company would fear competitors catching up if it slowed development unilaterally.

r005.rationale: It does not describe a warning that radical superintelligence is months away or propose coordinating the use of AI for protective activities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing would be to buy ourselves more time. If we had strong evidence that AI systems were starting to substantially accelerate AI research, I would want the companies and governments involved to take that very seriously and coordinate to slow down further development, especially if our ability to evaluate and control those systems wasn’t keeping pace.

There’s a distinction between thinking, “This could produce enormous benefits,” and thinking, “We’re ready to navigate this safely.” You can believe the first without believing the second. And once the process is moving very quickly, you may have much less opportunity to correct mistakes.

So I’d want a response that includes independent scrutiny of the evidence, much stronger security, and a credible ability to pause the most dangerous work. Ideally, we would have those arrangements in place beforehand, rather than trying to negotiate them in the middle of a crisis. The point of buying time would be to get better evidence that we can keep these systems under meaningful human control.

r001.rationale: The response mentions whether evaluation and control are keeping pace, but does not identify AI abilities outside AI research and development as a factor.

r002.rationale: It says rapid progress could reduce opportunities to correct mistakes, but does not state that automating AI research could compress decades of progress into months or years.

r003.rationale: It recommends slowing development and strengthening security, but does not recommend redirecting AI labor from research toward protective activities.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss a leading company's competitive disincentive to slow down because competitors could catch up.

r005.rationale: It does not describe a warning that radical superintelligence is months away or frame that warning as a window to coordinate protective AI use.
